American Association of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgeons.
Clinical Practice Guidelines for Oral and Maxillofacial
Surgery, 2012.7 (AGREE II Score: Unavailable)
•

This guideline does not specify which technique is superior to the
other in the management of mandibular angle fractures.

Author Commentary:

Background Mandibular angle fractures are very common and
prone to postsurgical complications.8 Proper fixation is essential
to ensure stability and to reduce the risk of complications. We systematically reviewed comparative effectiveness and safety of fix­
ation with 2 or 1 miniplates in patients with mandibular angle
fractures.

Methods We conducted a comprehensive search in PubMed, EMBASE,
the Cochrane Library, Elsevier text mining tool database including
National Institutes of Health RePORTER Grant database, and clinicaltrials.gov trial registry up to June 2016 and did a hand-search of the
reference lists. We searched for studies that investigated 2 or 1 miniplates
for the fixation of mandibular angle fractures in children or adults with
facial trauma.

Results We identified 2 systematic reviews of 3 RCTs and 7 observational studies and a subsequent publication of a single RCT.1–6 All studies
reported outcomes in adult patients with mandibular angle fractures.
We found no pediatric studies. Primary studies investigated 2 miniplates
placed on the external oblique ridge and on the ventral surface of the
mandible or a single miniplate placed on the external oblique ridge
with or without a locking system.
Low-quality evidence suggests that fixation with a single miniplate
placed on the external oblique ridge results in lower risk of failed hardware and overall risk of complications when compared with 2 miniplates
in adults with mandibular angle fracture (Table 1).1–5 Very low-quality
evidence suggests that internal fixation using a single locking miniplate
results in lower risk of postsurgical complications when compared with
a non-locking miniplate in adults with isolated unilateral mandibular
angle fractures.6

Limitations We downgraded the quality of evidence due to risk of
bias in the body of evidence and imprecision in treatment effects
from small studies. We found one guideline that acknowledged challenges in the management of mandibular angle fractures but does not
recommend specific fixation miniplates as superior to the others.7
The evidence regarding the effects of miniplate numbers on quality
of life, treatment utilization, or patient and provider satisfaction is
insufficient. Future research is needed to examine the comparative effectiveness and safety of fixation approaches in patients with
mandibular angle fractures and various demographic groups and
comorbidities.
Conclusions In adults with mandibular angle fracture, in order to
lower the risk of failed hardware and overall complications, clinicians
should use fixation with a single miniplate placed on the external
oblique ridge.

TEETH IN THE LINE OF MANDIBULAR ANGLE
FRACTURES (CHAPTER 1.14)
Clinical Question:
What are the comparative effectiveness and safety of retention versus
removal of teeth in the line of mandibular fractures?

Author Recommendation:
In adults with mandibular fractures treated with open reduction
and internal fixation (ORIF) with standard postoperative care, clinicians may choose to retain asymptomatic third molars to lower
the risk of inferior alveolar nerve injury and other complications.
Removal of erupted teeth should be performed at the surgeon’s
discretion.

American Association of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgeons.
Clinical Practice Guidelines for Oral and Maxillofacial
Surgery, 2012.25 (AGREE II Score: Unavailable)
•

This guideline does not specify which technique is superior to the
other in the management of teeth in the line of mandibular angle
fractures.

Author Commentary:

Background Mandibular angle fractures are very common and prone
to postsurgical complications.26 The presence of teeth on the fracture
line is associated with infections and other complications.25,27,28 We
systematically reviewed comparative effectiveness between retention
versus removal of teeth in adults with mandibular angle fractures.

Methods We conducted a comprehensive search in PubMed, EMBASE,
the Cochrane Library, Elsevier text mining tool database including
National Institutes of Health RePORTER Grant database, and clinicaltrials.gov trial registry up to March 2018 and did a hand-search of the
reference lists. We searched for studies of children or adults with teeth
in the line of mandibular fractures due to facial trauma.

Results We identified 1 RCT, 2 systematic reviews of observational
studies, and a total of 23 case series.1–24,29–52 All studies reported outcomes
in adult patients. We found no pediatric studies.
Very low-quality evidence from a single RCT suggests that retention
of asymptomatic third molars results in lower rates of inferior alveolar
nerve injury when compared with the removal of asymptomatic third
molars in adults with mandibular angle fractures treated with ORIF with
standard postoperative care (Table 1).1 This RCT concluded there was
no association between removal of teeth and postoperative infections.1
Multiple case series reported crude rates of the outcomes after retention or removal of teeth in the line of fracture. Low-quality evidence
suggests that retention is associated with lower rates of complications,

including malocclusion (Table 2). There is no association between the
risk of infection and the retention versus removal of teeth in the fracture line (Table 2). A tendency was seen toward lower rates of infection
and other complications associated with retention of teeth (Table 2).
Although no studies reported statistically significant increase in odds of
infections or other complications associated with retention of teeth, a
substantial heterogeneity existed in complication rates across case series
from various centers. Available information does not allow exploration
of heterogeneity by eruption of teeth, fracture severity, patient characteristics, surgical treatments, or provider characteristics (e.g., nosocomial infection rates in hospitals). We found only one case series that
reported outcomes in impacted versus erupted teeth (Fig. 1). Infection
and mechanical complications tended to be more frequent after the
retention of erupted teeth (Fig. 1). A systematic case review concluded
that erupted teeth with extensive periodontal damage, pericoronitis, or
periapical lesion should be removed.24 One case series demonstrated that
eruption of teeth and periodontal damage are associated with surgeon
decisions for postponed removal.23

Limitations We downgraded the quality of evidence due to risk of
bias in the body of evidence and imprecision in treatment effects from
small studies. We found one guideline that acknowledges challenges in
the management of teeth in the line of mandibular angle fractures, but
it does not recommend one therapeutic approach as being superior to
the others.25 Future research is needed to examine clear indications for
the retention or removal of teeth in the line of mandibular angle fractures in various demographic groups and in the presence of various
comorbidities.
Conclusions To lower the risk of inferior alveolar nerve injury and
other complications in adults with mandibular angle fractures treated
with ORIF with standard postoperative care, clinicians may choose to
retain asymptomatic third molars. Removal of erupted teeth should be
performed at the surgeon’s discretion.

COMPARATIVE BENEFITS AND HARMS OF OPEN
SURGICAL AND CLOSED REPAIR IN PATIENTS
WITH CONDYLAR FRACTURES AFTER TRAUMATIC
FACIAL INJURY (CHAPTER 1.15)
Clinical Question:
What are the comparative benefits and harms of open surgical repair
and closed repair in patients with condylar fractures after traumatic
facial injury?

Author Recommendation:
In adults with displaced condylar fractures after traumatic facial injury,
in order to reduce long-term temporomandibular joint (TMJ) pain
and improve function, clinicians should recommend open reduction
with internal fixation (ORIF) or endoscopically assisted open reduction
over closed treatments, with preventive measures against posttreatment
infection.

What Does the Evidence Conclude?

Quality of
Evidencea

Strength of
Recommendationsb

Low

Weak

Evidence suggests that ORIF results in lower rates of TMJ pain, lateral deviation during maximum interincisal
opening, and malocclusion and increases the range of protrusion and maximal interincisal opening, at the
expense of higher rates of posttreatment infection, when compared with closed treatments in adults with
displaced condylar fracture.

Very low

Weak

Evidence suggests that there are no differences in pain, function, or occlusion between surgical and endoscopically
assisted open reduction for adults with acute uni- or bilateral condyle fractures with displacement.

Guideline Recommendations:

American Association of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgeons.
Clinical Practice Guidelines for Oral and Maxillofacial
Surgery, 2012.7 (AGREE II Score: Unavailable)
•

•

This guideline recommends closed reduction in the following cases:
Nondisplaced or displaced fracture of a mandibular condyle where
form and/or function can be restored and there are no medical
contraindications to maxillomandibular fixations
Fracture dislocations or comminuted fractures in the growing child
where form and/or function can be restored
Medical and/or anesthetic contraindications to open reduction
This guideline recommends open reduction (including endoscopically assisted) in the following cases:
Fracture dislocation of a mandibular condyle
Mechanical interference with mandibular function by the condyle
or a foreign body
Condylar fractures with loss of anterior–posterior and vertical dimension that cannot be managed by closed reduction (e.g., edentulous
patient, multiple facial fractures)
Compound fracture
Displacement of a mandibular condyle into middle cranial fossa
Patient or surgeon preference for early or immediate mobilization
or function

International Bone Research Association Symposium for
Condylar Fracture Osteosynthesis. Position Paper, 2012.8
(AGREE II Score: Unavailable)
•

Experts developed a consensus that ORIF is a treatment of choice
for condylar base and neck fractures in adults, with a growing tendency to perform ORIF in condylar head fractures.

•
•

•

Endoscopic approaches should be considered for selected cases, such
as condylar base fractures with lateral displacement.
The experts also agreed to treat children (>12 years old) in the same
way as adults and to consider open reduction in severely displaced
and dislocated fractures even in younger children.
Experts recommend that nonsurgical treatment should be the first
choice for children <6 years of age. The decision to perform surgery
in children was based on factors influencing facial growth, appropriate age for ORIF, and disagreement about using resorbable materials
in children.

Author Commentary:

Background Condylar mandibular fractures are common in patients
with traumatic facial injuries, with remaining controversy regarding
the optimal open surgical or closed treatment options.7 Sustained patient
satisfaction with mandibular function and absence of pain, occlusion,
or impaired facial nerve function are among the most important treatment goals. We systematically reviewed the benefits and harms of open
surgical and closed treatments for condylar fractures in patients with
traumatic facial injury.

Methods Our team conducted a comprehensive search in PubMed,
EMBASE, the Cochrane Library, the Elsevier text mining tool database
including the National Institutes of Health RePORTER Grant database,
and the clinicaltrials.gov trial registry up to June 2016 and did a handsearch of the reference lists. We searched for studies of children or
adults with condylar facial fractures due to facial trauma and analyzed
the data separately according to fracture location and study design (e.g.,
RCTs and observational studies).

Results We identified 4 good-quality meta-analyses of 7 RCTs and 31
non-randomized studies that compared open surgical and closed

e36

APPENDIX 1 Evidence-Based Medicine

treatments for condylar fractures.1–4,9–14 We found one RCT that examined open surgical and endoscopic procedures for uni- or bilateral
condylar fractures.6 Primary studies enrolled adults with displaced unior bilateral condylar fractures and did not report the results by fracture
location (e.g., subcondylar or condylar) except with 2 RCTs that included
all adults with subcondylar fractures.3,5 Primary studies compared the
outcomes after open surgical procedure with those of fixation using 1
or 2 miniplates with various diameters.2 We found no pediatric studies.
Low-quality evidence suggests that ORIF results in lower rates of
TMJ pain, lateral deviation during maximum interincisal opening, and
malocclusion and increases the range of protrusion and maximal interincisal opening, at the expense of higher rates of posttreatment infection,
when compared with closed treatments in adults with displaced condylar
fractures (Table 1).1–4,6,9–14 Adults with displaced subcondylar fractures
experience less pain and better function after open surgery when compared with closed treatments.3,5 A relative reduction in the rates of TMJ
pain and malocclusion after open surgery is the same regardless of
study design or condylar fracture localization (statistical heterogeneity
is not significant).1–4,6,9–14
Very low-quality evidence from a single small RCT suggests that
there are no differences in pain, function, or occlusion between surgical
and endoscopically assisted open reduction for adults with acute uni- or
bilateral condyle fractures with displacement (Table 2).6

Limitations We downgraded the quality of evidence due to risk of
bias in the body of evidence and imprecision in treatment effects from
small studies. Observational studies did not use adjustment, and, therefore, patient and provider characteristics could contribute to differences
in outcomes between open surgical and closed treatments.
The guideline from the American Association of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgeons recommends open surgery only for dislocated mandibular condyle fractures that cannot be managed by closed reduction,
for compound fractures, or for fractures with a displacement of a mandibular condyle into the middle cranial fossa.7 The experts from the
International Bone Research Association recommend ORIF as a treatment of choice for condylar base and neck fractures.8 Future research
is needed to examine the comparative effectiveness and safety of various
surgical, endoscopic, and conservative techniques in patients with facial
trauma and various demographic groups and comorbidities.
Conclusions In adults with displaced condylar fractures after traumatic
facial injury, in order to reduce long-term TMJ pain and improve function, clinicians should recommend ORIF or endoscopically assisted
open reduction over closed treatments, with preventive measures against
posttreatment infection.

Evidence suggests that there are no differences in functional recovery, complications, or infections between open

Insufficient

Weak

Evidence suggests that the majority of adults with atrophic and edentulous mandibular fractures experience clinical

comorbidities unreported in the studies, surgeon experience and training, and the quality of care in different
institutions.

Guideline Recommendations:

American Association of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgeons.
Clinical Practice Guidelines for Oral and Maxillofacial
Surgery, 2012.19 (AGREE II Score: Unavailable)
•

This guideline does not specify which technique is superior in the
management of atrophic and edentulous mandibular fractures.

Author Commentary:

Background Traumatic mandibular fractures in aging adults with
frequent multimorbidity are associated with higher mortality and longer
hospital stay.20 Atrophic edentulous mandibles in the elderly are easy
to break and difficult to fixate and heal.21 The degree of atrophy is
categorized according to mandibular height.13 More severe atrophy is
associated with higher risk of complications and poor function.22 Most
experts practice closed reduction over open reduction procedure to
reduce the risk of postsurgical morbidity.21 There is controversy regarding whether the optimal fixation procedure is load-bearing osteosynthesis
using rigid locking reconstruction plates, load-sharing osteosynthesis
with miniplates, or semi-rigid Champy fixation.21 We systematically
reviewed the comparative effectiveness and safety between fixation
techniques in adults with traumatic fractures of atrophic edentulous
mandible.

Methods We conducted a comprehensive search in PubMed, EMBASE,
the Cochrane Library, Elsevier text mining tool database including
National Institutes of Health RePORTER Grant database, and clinicaltrials.gov trial registry up to July 2016 and did a hand-search of the
reference lists. We searched for the studies of older adults with atrophic
and edentulous traumatic mandibular fractures.

Results We identified 1 high-quality Cochrane review,23 6 narrative
reviews, and 21 publications of case reports and case series.1–18,21,24–31
The high-quality Cochrane review found no randomized trials
examining fracture management in edentulous mandibles.23 Primary
uncontrolled case series reported patient outcomes in older adults with
different degree of mandibular atrophy treated with load-bearing or
load-sharing fixation techniques and autologous bone grafting. We
calculated outcome rates with 95% confidence intervals by fixation
method and degree of atrophy, when reported in the studies.
Very low-quality evidence from a single small controlled case series
suggests that there are no differences in functional recovery, complications, or infections between open reduction and internal rigid fixation
using 2.0 mm versus 2.4 mm large profile locking systems in adults
with atrophic edentulous mandibular fractures (Table 1).1
Uncontrolled case series suggest that more than 90% of the patients
had complete functional and morphological restoration after locking

APPENDIX 1 Evidence-Based Medicine
reconstruction plates and autogenous bone grafting or rigid fixation
using horseshoe-shaped Kirschner wire with a 2 mm diameter after
conservative reduction with the Interrami intraoral Kirschner wire fixation (IRIF) technique (Table 2).3,4 The other case series reported only
50% complete functional and morphological restoration after loadbearing osteosynthesis plates with locking screws (Table 2).2 Available
patient or procedure characteristics could not explain differences in
recovery rate in a very small patient sample.
The majority of patients across institutions experienced primary
healing and clinical bony union (Table 1). However, we noticed a substantial variability in complication rate across institutions not associated
with specific fixation technique or severity of mandibular atrophy.
Unreported patient comorbidities, surgeon experience and training,
and quality of care in different institutions may contribute to variability
in complication rates.
Case reports demonstrate that load-bearing reconstruction plate
combined with autogenous bone graft resulted in complete functional
and morphological restoration in 2 patients who failed load-sharing
miniplate fixation.29,31

Limitations We downgraded the quality of evidence due to risk of
bias in the body of evidence and imprecision in treatment effects from
a small controlled case series. We did not grade the quality of evidence
from uncontrolled case series, because such studies do not provide
valid evidence for decision-making. Wide 95% confidence intervals of
outcome rates and substantial variability in complication rates across
single institutions precluded calculation of valid average rates of the
outcomes.
We found one guideline that acknowledges challenges in the management of mandibular fractures in patients with bone atrophy and
other comorbidities but does not recommend one therapeutic approach
as superior to the others.19 Future research is needed to examine comparative effectiveness and safety from fixation approaches in elderly
patients with traumatic atrophic and edentulous mandibular fractures
and various demographic groups and comorbidities.
Conclusions Evidence suggests that the majority of adults with atrophic and edentulous mandibular fractures experience clinical bone
union after either load-bearing or load-sharing fixation. However,
complication rates vary, likely due to patient comorbidities unreported
in the studies, surgeon experience and training, and the quality of care
in different institutions.

confidence interval; GRADE, Grading of Recommendations Assessment,
Development and Evaluation; NR, not reported; OR, odds ratio;

Reporting Tools https://federalreporter.nih.gov/..
